title: June 1–September 12, 1897
scope_note: Expansion in progress: 62 sourced items across June 1–September 12, 1897. The current pre-August tranche now reaches into the pre-treaty information world with the June 7 launch of Ka Ahalono o Hawaii, follows the June 16 annexation-treaty shock and Liliʻuokalani's June 17 protest, preserves ordinary-life signals, and adds a July 3 Ke Aloha Aina prayer invoking the Kumulipo before the August 21 unity mele.

items.english_close: Ka Ahalono o Hawaii, the name of a new Hawaiian-language newspaper.
items.feed_rendering: A new Hawaiian-language paper enters Honolulu's information world: William White starts Ka Ahalono o Hawaii.
items.voice_evidence: This is a reconstructed publication event, not a quotation from the paper. Historian Ronald Williams Jr.'s archival column, drawing on newspaper, manuscript, correspondence, and other archival collections, reported on June 11, 1897 that William White had started Ka Ahalono o Hawaii 'this past Monday,' placing the launch on June 7. The Hawaiian field preserves only the newspaper title rather than inventing article text.
items.source_label: Ka Wai Ola, February 2009, 'Kela Mea Kela Mea' by Ronald Williams Jr., archival note reconstructing the June 7, 1897 launch of Ka Ahalono o Hawaii
items.translation_basis: The feed wording is a modern event summary derived from the archival research note. No unrecovered article interior or first-person newspaper voice is reconstructed.

items.hawaiian: ua kakauinoaia ma Wasinetona ... e haawi ana hoi i keia mau mokupuni ... malalo hoi o ka mana o Amerika Huipuia
items.english_close: A treaty had been signed in Washington to cede these islands under the authority of the United States.
items.feed_rendering: A treaty has been signed in Washington to hand Hawaiʻi to the United States. Liliʻuokalani moves to protest it the next day.
items.voice_evidence: The Hawaiian wording comes from Liliʻuokalani's June 17 protest describing the annexation treaty signed the previous day. This card marks the treaty event through the Queen's documented reaction rather than pretending it is a separate newspaper eyewitness report.
items.source_label: Ke Aloha Aina, July 10, 1897, p. 6, preserving Liliʻuokalani's June 17 protest and its description of the treaty signed June 16
items.translation_basis: Close English derived from the public-domain Hawaiian protest transcription; the treaty date is independently confirmed by U.S. State Department historical records.
items.information_lag_note: The annexation treaty was signed June 16 in Washington. Ke Aloha Aina printed the Hawaiian text of Liliʻuokalani's June 17 protest on July 10, so this feed preserves the gap instead of making the information instantaneous.

items.hawaiian: ma keia ke kue aku nei Au i ke aponoia ana
items.english_close: By this I protest its ratification.
items.feed_rendering: I formally protest ratification of this treaty.
items.voice_evidence: The source is Liliʻuokalani's formal written protest delivered to U.S. Secretary of State John Sherman on June 17, one day after the treaty was signed.
items.source_label: UH Mānoa Library, Liliʻuokalani protest to William McKinley, June 17, 1897; Hawaiian newspaper report preserved with the document collection
items.translation_basis: Close English derived from the Hawaiian wording preserved in the July 10 Ke Aloha Aina publication and checked against the archival English protest.
items.information_lag_note: The protest was delivered in Washington on June 17. Ke Aloha Aina printed its Hawaiian text on July 10, twenty-three days later.

items.hawaiian: he hana hewa ia i na kanaka a hapa Hawaii pu
items.english_close: It is a wrong against Native Hawaiian and part-Hawaiian people.
items.feed_rendering: This treaty is a wrong against Native Hawaiians and part-Hawaiians.
items.voice_evidence: Liliʻuokalani explicitly characterizes the treaty as a wrong against Hawaiian people rather than treating annexation as a neutral transfer between governments.
items.source_label: Ke Aloha Aina, July 10, 1897, p. 6, Hawaiian text of Liliʻuokalani's June 17 protest
items.translation_basis: Close English derived directly from the short Hawaiian clause in the public-domain protest text.
items.information_lag_note: The protest was made June 17 and printed in Hawaiian by Ke Aloha Aina on July 10.

items.hawaiian: aole loa lakou i kuka pu ia aku
items.feed_rendering: My people were never consulted about breaking Hawaiʻi's independence.
items.voice_evidence: In the surrounding protest, Liliʻuokalani contrasts roughly forty thousand of her people with the small group claiming authority to destroy Hawaiian independence, making lack of consent the point of the passage.
items.source_label: Ke Aloha Aina, July 10, 1897, p. 6, Hawaiian text of Liliʻuokalani's June 17 protest
items.translation_basis: Close English derived from the preserved Hawaiian clause; surrounding context comes from the same public-domain protest text.
items.information_lag_note: The consent argument was written June 17 and reached Ke Aloha Aina readers in this printed Hawaiian form on July 10.

items.hawaiian: e unuhi aku i ua kuikahi la
items.feed_rendering: I ask the President to withdraw the treaty from further consideration.
items.voice_evidence: The closing section directly asks the U.S. president to withdraw the treaty from further consideration. The separate request to the Senate is preserved as its own atomic record rather than collapsed into this one.
items.source_label: UH Mānoa Library, Liliʻuokalani protest to William McKinley, June 17, 1897
items.translation_basis: The short Hawaiian imperative is preserved in the July 10 Ke Aloha Aina text; the archival English protest independently confirms the requested withdrawal.
items.information_lag_note: The request was made June 17 in Washington and later circulated in Hawaiian through Ke Aloha Aina on July 10.

items.hawaiian: e hoole i ke apono ana i ua kuikahi la
items.feed_rendering: I ask the United States Senate to refuse ratification of the treaty.
items.voice_evidence: Immediately after asking the U.S. president to withdraw the treaty, Liliʻuokalani separately asks the United States Senate to refuse its approval. Keeping the two requests separate preserves their different institutional targets.
items.source_label: Ke Aloha Aina, July 10, 1897, p. 6, Hawaiian text of Liliʻuokalani's June 17 protest
items.translation_basis: Close English is derived from the preserved Hawaiian clause and checked against the archival English protest's request that the Senate decline ratification.
items.information_lag_note: The Senate request was made June 17 in Washington and printed in Hawaiian by Ke Aloha Aina on July 10, twenty-three days later.

items.hawaiian: He lono lauahea kai hulihali ia mai e ka makani Moae
items.english_close: Hearsay news has been carried in on the Moaʻe wind.
items.feed_rendering: Word on the Moaʻe wind: the lāhui's young musicians may hold a concert at Kaumakapili on July 3. They're practicing now on Nuʻuanu Street.
items.voice_evidence: The item explicitly labels itself hearsay and promises another notice once confirmed, giving the post a cautious rumor-network quality rather than certainty.
items.source_label: Ke Aloha Aina, June 19, 1897, p. 7, 'Ke Oiaio Hoi,' Hawaiian transcription in UH Mānoa IHLRT
items.translation_basis: Feed wording is independently derived from the public-domain Hawaiian transcription. IHLRT provides a scholarly translation for semantic checking; its wording is not reproduced here.

items.hawaiian: Na Ike Nohona Home ... Ka Waiwai o ka Ike Mele ... Ka Ike Hana maoli
items.english_close: Domestic sciences ... the value of musical knowledge ... practical arts.
items.feed_rendering: Kamehameha Girls' School graduation night includes talks on domestic sciences, music, practical arts, childhood, and life at Kamehameha.
items.voice_evidence: The newspaper's graduation program lists student presentations by topic rather than attributing a single quoted speech. The feed keeps this as a program notice, not a fabricated student voice.
items.source_label: Ka Nupepa Kuokoa, July 2, 1897, p. 2, report on the June 29 Kamehameha School for Girls graduation
items.translation_basis: Program topic titles are preserved bilingually in the historical report; feed wording summarizes the program without inventing remarks by the students.
items.information_lag_note: The graduation occurred June 29 and Ka Nupepa Kuokoa reported it on July 2, a three-day event-to-publication lag.

items.hawaiian: He Pule Ola Hawaii — Po-wale-ho-i-e. Hanau ka po ia Hawaii He Aupuni Moi.
items.english_close: Prayer for the life of Hawaiʻi — Only night. Night gave birth to Hawaiʻi, a Kingdom.
items.feed_rendering: Ke Aloha Aina reaches into the Kumulipo during the annexation crisis: night gives birth to Hawaiʻi, a kingdom.
items.voice_evidence: Noenoe K. Silva's archival analysis quotes Ke Aloha Aina reproducing the opening of the Kumulipo and appending these lines under the title 'He Pule Ola Hawaii.' The paper explained the creation imagery as fitting a moment when the people lacked stable government. This is treated as an editorial-cultural act by the publication, not as words attributed to a named individual.
items.source_label: Noenoe K. Silva, Aloha Betrayed, quoting Ke Aloha Aina, July 3, 1897, 'He Pule Ola Hawaii' and its use of the Kumulipo during the anti-annexation struggle
items.translation_basis: Close English is derived from the short historical Hawaiian passage quoted in the scholarly source and checked against Silva's translation.

items.feed_rendering: One thought. One aloha. One heart. Keep the peace.
items.voice_evidence: Ke Aloha Aina printed this line twice in Samuel K. Kamakaia's mele 'Nai Wale No Oukou Aoʻe Pau.' The surrounding third stanza repeats unity of thought, aloha, and heart before closing again with this instruction to keep the peace.
items.source_label: Ke Aloha Aina, August 21, 1897, p. 7, 'Nai Wale No Oukou Aoʻe Pau,' transcribed by Nūpepa Hawaiʻi
items.translation_basis: Close English is independently derived from the source-facing Hawaiian. Nūpepa Hawaiʻi also identifies the repeated line as 'Keep the peace.'
